subject: Architecture
title: Low-Carbon Concrete: Fixing the Worst Offender
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Low-Carbon Concrete: Fixing the Worst Offender.

hook.text: If the cement industry were a country, it would be the world's third-largest emitter of carbon dioxide.

buildup.text: Making portland cement requires heating limestone to 2,700°F — a chemical reaction that releases CO₂.

discovery.text: Replacing 30% of cement with fly ash or slag — industrial byproducts — cuts emissions dramatically.

twist.text: CarbonCure injects captured CO₂ into fresh concrete, where it mineralizes and strengthens the mix.

climax.text: Companies are developing concrete that cures with CO₂ instead of releasing it — potentially carbon-negative.

punchline.text: The dirtiest material in construction could become part of the climate solution.

quiz.question: What does CarbonCure technology do to concrete?
options: Replaces cement with recycled plastic fibers
Injects captured CO₂ that mineralizes and strengthens the mix
Cures concrete using solar heat instead of kilns

details.summary: Cement production generates 8% of global CO2 emissions — more than aviation. Low-carbon alternatives replace Portland cement with industrial byproducts like fly ash, slag, and calcined clay, or use novel chemistries that absorb CO2 during curing instead of emitting it during manufacturing.
details.whyItMatters: Concrete is the world's most used manufactured material, and its carbon footprint is enormous. Reducing cement's emissions is one of the single largest opportunities for climate impact in the entire construction industry.
takeaways: Cement production generates 8% of global CO2 emissions
Fly ash, slag, and clay can replace Portland cement partially
Some novel cements absorb CO2 during curing instead of emitting it

faq.question: Why does cement produce so much CO2?
faq.answer: The chemical process of making clinker (the active ingredient in cement) decomposes limestone, releasing CO2 as a chemical byproduct. Kilns also burn fossil fuels at 1,450°C.

faq.question: Can low-carbon concrete perform as well as conventional?
faq.answer: Yes, in most applications. Blended cements using 30-50% alternative materials match or exceed conventional concrete strength. Higher replacement ratios require more careful mix design.
